claim: At the time of writing (September 2022), 80% of the citizens of low-income countries are still waiting for their first dose of a COVID-19 vaccine.
source: At the time of writing, and a year after Guterres gave his speech, 80% of the citizens of low-income countries are still waiting for their first dose of a COVID-19 vaccine, whereas in high-income countries, almost 80% of citizens are vaccinated.
evidence: The claim cites data about vaccination rates in low-income countries at the time of writing, which is supported by references to data sources (Mathieu et al., 2021; Our World in Data, 2022).

claim: In high-income countries, almost 80% of citizens are vaccinated against COVID-19.
source: At the time of writing, and a year after Guterres gave his speech, 80% of the citizens of low-income countries are still waiting for their first dose of a COVID-19 vaccine, whereas in high-income countries, almost 80% of citizens are vaccinated.
evidence: The claim cites vaccination rate data for high-income countries, supported by references to data sources (Mathieu et al., 2021; Our World in Data, 2022).

claim: In the past 12 months, the total number of vaccine doses administered per 100 people amounts to almost 100 in high-income countries and to only 27 in low-income countries.
source: In the past 12 months, the total number of vaccine doses administered per 100 people amounts to almost 100 in high-income countries and to only 27 in low-income countries (Mathieu et al., 2021; Our World in Data, 2022).
evidence: The claim provides specific numerical data about vaccine doses administered, with citations to data sources.

claim: Unequal access to vaccination leads to high rates of transmission, severe infections, and deaths in parts of the world where health care capacity is the lowest.
source: From an ethical perspective, unequal access to vaccination leads to high rates of transmission, severe infections, and deaths in those parts of the world where health care capacity is the lowest.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to scholarly work discussing health inequities (Godlee, 2021; Katz et al., 2021; Krause et al., 2021; Wagner et al., 2021).

claim: Unequal vaccine distribution aggravates existing health inequities between the Global South and North.
source: This aggravates existing health inequities between the Global South and North (Godlee, 2021; Katz et al., 2021; Krause et al., 2021; Wagner et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to scholarly literature on health inequities.

claim: A scenario where the 50 richest countries used all available vaccines would lead to twice as many COVID-19 deaths compared to a scenario where vaccines were allocated proportionally to population size.
source: A recent modeling study compared two hypothetical scenarios – one in which the 50 richest countries used all available vaccines and one in which vaccines were allocated to all countries proportionally to their population size – finding that the former scenario would lead to twice as many COVID-19 deaths (Herzog et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is based on a modeling study cited in the text.

claim: Constrained access to COVID-19 vaccines in low- and middle-income countries would reduce the global GDP by US$ 153 billion each year.
source: The RAND Corporation estimates that constrained access to COVID-19 vaccines in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) would reduce the global GDP by US$ 153 billion each year, including a loss of US$ 56 billion in the European Union and United States combined (Hafner et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites an economic estimate from the RAND Corporation.

claim: Constrained access to COVID-19 vaccines in LMICs would result in a loss of US$ 56 billion in the European Union and United States combined.
source: The RAND Corporation estimates that constrained access to COVID-19 vaccines in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) would reduce the global GDP by US$ 153 billion each year, including a loss of US$ 56 billion in the European Union and United States combined (Hafner et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites an economic estimate from the RAND Corporation.

claim: Every US dollar spent on supplying vaccines to LMICs would yield a return of US$ 4.8.
source: Put differently, every US dollar spent on supplying vaccines to LMICs would yield a return of US$ 4.8 (Hafner et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim cites an economic analysis from the RAND Corporation.

claim: Unmitigated COVID-19 transmissions in some parts of the world create evolutionary reservoirs from which new SARS-CoV-2 variants arise.
source: Unmitigated COVID-19 transmissions in some parts of the world create evolutionary reservoirs from which new SARS-CoV-2 variants arise, increasing the risk of immune escape - for both vaccine-induced and natural immunity - and of other phenotypic changes that could lead to greater virulence (Saad-Roy et al., 2021; Telenti et al., 2021; van Oosterhout et al., 2021; Wagner et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to virological literature.

claim: Unmitigated COVID-19 transmissions increase the risk of immune escape for both vaccine-induced and natural immunity.
source: Unmitigated COVID-19 transmissions in some parts of the world create evolutionary reservoirs from which new SARS-CoV-2 variants arise, increasing the risk of immune escape - for both vaccine-induced and natural immunity - and of other phenotypic changes that could lead to greater virulence (Saad-Roy et al., 2021; Telenti et al., 2021; van Oosterhout et al., 2021; Wagner et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to virological literature.

claim: The globally unequal distribution of COVID-19 vaccines is partly a consequence of widespread vaccine nationalism in high-income countries.
source: The globally unequal distribution of COVID-19 vaccines, including the stockpiling of vaccine doses for their own citizens, is partly a consequence of widespread vaccine nationalism in high-income countries (Harman et al., 2021; Herzog et al., 2021; Wagner et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on vaccine nationalism.

claim: Several governments have made bilateral purchasing agreements with vaccine manufacturers outside of COVAX, which has substantially weakened COVAX's collective purchasing power.
source: However, several governments have resorted to making bilateral purchasing agreements with vaccine manufacturers outside of COVAX, which has substantially weakened the initiatives' collective purchasing power (Kim, 2021; Wouters et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to literature on COVAX and vaccine procurement.

claim: 25% of announced EU vaccine doses to COVAX have not yet been donated.
source: Moreover, out of those vaccine doses that were initially announced as donations to COVAX by high-income countries, substantial proportions – 25% of announced EU doses and almost 50% of announced US doses – have in fact not yet been donated (WHO ACT-Accelerator Hub; Our World in Data, 2022; Mathieu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites data from WHO and Our World in Data about vaccine donations.

claim: Almost 50% of announced US vaccine doses to COVAX have not yet been donated.
source: Moreover, out of those vaccine doses that were initially announced as donations to COVAX by high-income countries, substantial proportions – 25% of announced EU doses and almost 50% of announced US doses – have in fact not yet been donated (WHO ACT-Accelerator Hub; Our World in Data, 2022; Mathieu et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites data from WHO and Our World in Data about vaccine donations.

claim: Decision-makers in high-income countries are likely to exhibit vaccine nationalism if they believe there is little public support for giving COVID-19 vaccines to poorer regions.
source: Decision-makers in high-income countries are likely to exhibit vaccine nationalism and refrain from vaccine donations if they believe there is little public support for giving COVID-19 vaccines to poorer regions of the world (Clarke et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation and represents an inference about political behavior.

claim: A majority of studies on COVID-19 vaccine allocation examined public opinion on prioritisation within high-income countries when vaccine availability was still heavily constrained.
source: A majority of these studies examined public opinion on prioritisation within high-income countries and when COVID-19 vaccine availability was still heavily constrained in those countries (Duch et al., 2021; Gollust et al., 2020; Knotz et al., 2021; Luyten et al., 2020; Persad et al., 2021; Reeskens et al., 2021; Sprengholz et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: Studies revealed substantial public support for prioritising frontline healthcare workers and clinically vulnerable groups for COVID-19 vaccination.
source: Based on data from online surveys and survey experiments, the studies revealed substantial public support for prioritising frontline healthcare workers and clinically vulnerable groups (Duch et al., 2021; Persad et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from cited studies.

claim: Around 50% of participants in seven high-income countries supported global allocation schemes that would give priority to countries that could not afford to purchase vaccines.
source: One online survey conducted in seven high-income countries found that around 50% of participants generally supported global allocation schemes that would give priority to the countries that could not afford to purchase vaccines (Clarke et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites findings from a specific survey study.

claim: 40% of US respondents were in favour of donating at least 10% of nationally purchased vaccines to poorer countries.
source: Another survey conducted in the US found that 40% of respondents were in favour of donating at least 10% of the nationally purchased vaccines to poorer countries.
evidence: The claim cites findings from a US survey study (Guidry et al., 2021).

claim: Support for vaccine donations to poorer countries was less pronounced among older US respondents.
source: Support was less pronounced among older respondents – a group that is at greater risk of severe disease progression if infected (Guidry et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites findings from a US survey study.

claim: German survey participants displayed a strong preference for a vaccine alliance exclusively composed of EU states.
source: The authors found that participants displayed a strong preference for an alliance exclusively composed of EU states.
evidence: The claim cites findings from a German survey study (Vanhuysse et al., 2021).

claim: German participants were more supportive of vaccine alliances if the national cost of participation was lower and national vaccine coverage higher.
source: More importantly, the authors found that participants were more supportive of vaccine alliances if the national cost of participation was lower and national vaccine coverage higher, suggesting that participants' preferences were significantly shaped by self-interest (Vanhuysse et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites findings from a German survey study.

claim: In a discrete choice experiment conducted in Germany and the US, participants expressed a strong preference for prioritising vaccine allocation to countries with a higher number of COVID-19 deaths and fewer intensive care unit beds.
source: In contrast, in a discrete choice experiment conducted in Germany and the US, participants in both countries expressed a strong preference for prioritising vaccine allocation to countries with a higher number of COVID-19 deaths and fewer intensive care unit beds, even when they were asked to imagine that they or a vulnerable family member were still waiting for the COVID-19 vaccine (Klumpp et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites findings from a discrete choice experiment study.

claim: No previous study to date has exclusively sampled participants who were still waiting for their first COVID-19 vaccine dose when participating in the survey experiment.
source: Notably, no previous study to date has exclusively sampled participants who were still waiting for their first COVID-19 vaccine dose when participating in the survey experiment.
evidence: The claim is a statement about the novelty of the current study's methodology based on review of existing literature.

claim: The German survey was launched at the height of the third wave in April 2021.
source: The German survey was launched at the height of the third wave in April 2021; the other five surveys were carried out in June 2021, coinciding with a phase of low case numbers in each country (see Figure 1).
evidence: The claim states the timing of the German survey and is supported by reference to Figure 1 showing COVID-19 case data.

claim: The five non-German surveys were carried out in June 2021, coinciding with a phase of low case numbers in each country.
source: The German survey was launched at the height of the third wave in April 2021; the other five surveys were carried out in June 2021, coinciding with a phase of low case numbers in each country (see Figure 1).
evidence: The claim states the timing of the surveys and is supported by reference to Figure 1 showing COVID-19 case data.

claim: Discrete choice experiments are used to measure the relative importance of different characteristics that respondents weigh against each other when making certain choices.
source: Discrete choice experiments (DCEs) are used to measure the relative importance of different characteristics that respondents weigh against each other when making certain choices (Mangham et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim defines DCE methodology with a citation.

claim: DCEs are based on the assumption that respondents express their preferences by choosing the alternative associated with the highest individual benefits or utility.
source: DCEs have emerged from the theoretical tradition of random utility theory and are based on the assumption that respondents express their preferences by choosing the alternative associated with the highest individual benefits or utility (Hall et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim describes the theoretical basis of DCEs with a citation.

claim: DCEs have advantages over other stated preference techniques because they more closely mimic real-world choice scenarios, reduce cognitive complexity for respondents, and can elicit implicit preferences.
source: DCEs have advantages over other stated preference techniques, such as ranking or rating exercises, because they (i) more closely mimic real-world choice scenarios, (ii) reduce the cognitive complexity for respondents, and (iii) can elicit implicit preferences (Mangham et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim describes advantages of DCEs with a citation.

claim: Participants were only eligible to participate in the survey experiment if they had not yet been vaccinated against COVID-19 at the time of the survey and indicated that they were willing to get vaccinated.
source: Participants were only eligible to participate in the survey experiment if they (1) had not yet been vaccinated against COVID-19 at the time of the survey and (2) indicated that they were willing to get vaccinated.
evidence: The claim describes the eligibility criteria for the study.

claim: Power calculations for the discrete choice experiment indicated an optimal sample size of n=2,061 respondents per country.
source: Power calculations for the discrete choice experiment indicated an optimal sample size of n=2,061 respondents per country (de Bekker-Grob et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim states the target sample size based on power calculations with a citation.

claim: The required sample size was only reached in Germany due to the earlier timing of the data collection and budget constraints.
source: However, the rapidly evolving pandemic situation in combination with conditional eligibility on vaccination status (see above) only allowed us to reach the required sample size in Germany due to the earlier timing of the data collection as well as budget constraints.
evidence: The claim explains why the target sample size was not reached in all countries.

claim: Sample sizes in the non-German countries ranged from 670 in Poland to 925 in Spain, resulting in a total sample size of 6030 eligible responses.
source: Sample sizes in the remaining countries ranged from 670 in Poland to 925 in Spain, resulting in a total sample size of 6030 eligible responses.
evidence: The claim provides specific sample size data.

claim: In France, Italy, Spain, and Sweden, respondents on average chose the hypothetical candidate from the Global South over the hypothetical candidate from their own country to receive the vaccine first.
source: In France, Italy, Spain, and Sweden, respondents, on average, chose the hypothetical candidate from the Global South over the hypothetical candidate from their own country to receive the vaccine first (Spain: OR: 1.79, 95% CI: 1.55–2.06; Italy: OR: 1.74, 95% CI: 1.50–2.01; Sweden: OR: 1.43, 95% CI: 1.24–1.65; France: OR: 1.37, 95% CI: 1.18–1.59; all p-values <0.001).
evidence: The claim presents statistical results from the DCE with specific odds ratios and confidence intervals.

claim: Spanish respondents had 1.79 times higher odds of choosing a candidate from the Global South to receive the vaccine (95% CI: 1.55–2.06, p<0.001).
source: In France, Italy, Spain, and Sweden, respondents, on average, chose the hypothetical candidate from the Global South over the hypothetical candidate from their own country to receive the vaccine first (Spain: OR: 1.79, 95% CI: 1.55–2.06; Italy: OR: 1.74, 95% CI: 1.50–2.01; Sweden: OR: 1.43, 95% CI: 1.24–1.65; France: OR: 1.37, 95% CI: 1.18–1.59; all p-values <0.001).
evidence: The claim presents specific statistical results from the DCE for Spain.

claim: Italian respondents had 1.74 times higher odds of choosing a candidate from the Global South to receive the vaccine (95% CI: 1.50–2.01, p<0.001).
source: In France, Italy, Spain, and Sweden, respondents, on average, chose the hypothetical candidate from the Global South over the hypothetical candidate from their own country to receive the vaccine first (Spain: OR: 1.79, 95% CI: 1.55–2.06; Italy: OR: 1.74, 95% CI: 1.50–2.01; Sweden: OR: 1.43, 95% CI: 1.24–1.65; France: OR: 1.37, 95% CI: 1.18–1.59; all p-values <0.001).
evidence: The claim presents specific statistical results from the DCE for Italy.

claim: Swedish respondents had 1.43 times higher odds of choosing a candidate from the Global South to receive the vaccine (95% CI: 1.24–1.65, p<0.001).
source: In France, Italy, Spain, and Sweden, respondents, on average, chose the hypothetical candidate from the Global South over the hypothetical candidate from their own country to receive the vaccine first (Spain: OR: 1.79, 95% CI: 1.55–2.06; Italy: OR: 1.74, 95% CI: 1.50–2.01; Sweden: OR: 1.43, 95% CI: 1.24–1.65; France: OR: 1.37, 95% CI: 1.18–1.59; all p-values <0.001).
evidence: The claim presents specific statistical results from the DCE for Sweden.

claim: French respondents had 1.37 times higher odds of choosing a candidate from the Global South to receive the vaccine (95% CI: 1.18–1.59, p<0.001).
source: In France, Italy, Spain, and Sweden, respondents, on average, chose the hypothetical candidate from the Global South over the hypothetical candidate from their own country to receive the vaccine first (Spain: OR: 1.79, 95% CI: 1.55–2.06; Italy: OR: 1.74, 95% CI: 1.50–2.01; Sweden: OR: 1.43, 95% CI: 1.24–1.65; France: OR: 1.37, 95% CI: 1.18–1.59; all p-values <0.001).
evidence: The claim presents specific statistical results from the DCE for France.

claim: German respondents showed significantly lower odds of choosing candidates from the Global South to receive the vaccine (OR: 0.69, 95% CI: 0.62–0.76, p<0.001).
source: For German respondents, we observe the opposite pattern: candidates from the Global South had significantly lower odds of being chosen to receive the vaccine (OR: 0.69, 95% CI: 0.62–0.76, p-value <0.001).
evidence: The claim presents specific statistical results from the DCE for Germany.

claim: In Poland, a candidate's country of residence neither increased nor decreased the odds of being chosen to receive the vaccine (OR: 0.99, 95% CI: 0.86–1.15).
source: In Poland, a candidate's country of residence neither increased nor decreased the odds of being chosen to receive the vaccine (OR: 0.99, 95% CI: 0.86–1.15).
evidence: The claim presents specific statistical results from the DCE for Poland.

claim: In all six countries, the odds of being chosen to receive the vaccine were between two and almost six times higher for a candidate with an increased COVID-19 mortality risk, relative to a candidate with an average risk.
source: For the attribute of COVID-19 mortality risk, we observe a similar pattern in all surveyed countries: The odds of being chosen to receive the vaccine were between two and almost six times higher for a candidate with an increased COVID-19 mortality risk, relative to a candidate with an average risk.
evidence: The claim summarizes statistical results across all countries regarding mortality risk.

claim: The effect of increased mortality risk on vaccine allocation preference was even more pronounced for a candidate with a strongly increased mortality risk, ranging from OR: 4.35 (95% CI: 3.65–5.19) in Poland to OR: 14.20 (95% CI: 11.75–17.17) in Sweden.
source: The effect was even more pronounced for a candidate with a strongly increased mortality risk (ranging from OR: 4.35, 95% CI: 3.65–5.19 in Poland to OR: 14.20, 95% CI: 11.75–17.17 in Sweden; all p-values <0.001).
evidence: The claim presents specific statistical results regarding strongly increased mortality risk.

claim: In all countries, employed candidates who lost income due to the pandemic and candidates who were employed in essential services were significantly more likely to be chosen to receive the vaccine when compared to unemployed candidates.
source: For employment status and age, we also observed largely similar patterns across countries: First, employed candidates who lost income due to the pandemic and candidates who were employed in essential services were significantly more likely to be chosen to receive the vaccine when compared to unemployed candidates.
evidence: The claim summarizes statistical results across all countries regarding employment status.

claim: In all countries, 40-year-old candidates had slightly higher odds of being chosen to receive the vaccine than 20- or 60-year-old candidates.
source: Second, in all countries, 40-year-old candidates had slightly higher odds of being chosen to receive the vaccine than 20- or 60-year-old candidates.
evidence: The claim summarizes statistical results across all countries regarding age.

claim: The odds of choosing the candidate from the Global South were significantly higher for female respondents (OR of interaction: 1.22, 95% CI: 1.10–1.36, p<0.001).
source: The odds of choosing the candidate from the Global South rather than the candidate from the respondents' own country (all else equal) were significantly higher for female (OR of interaction: 1.22, 95% CI: 1.10–1.36, p-value <0.001) and more educated (OR of interaction: 1.63, 95% CI: 1.46–1.82, p-value <0.001) respondents, and significantly lower for older respondents (above 45 years) (OR of interaction: 0.68, 95% CI: 0.61–0.76, p-value <0.001).
evidence: The claim presents specific statistical results from the heterogeneity analysis for gender.

claim: The odds of choosing the candidate from the Global South were significantly higher for more educated respondents (OR of interaction: 1.63, 95% CI: 1.46–1.82, p<0.001).
source: The odds of choosing the candidate from the Global South rather than the candidate from the respondents' own country (all else equal) were significantly higher for female (OR of interaction: 1.22, 95% CI: 1.10–1.36, p-value <0.001) and more educated (OR of interaction: 1.63, 95% CI: 1.46–1.82, p-value <0.001) respondents, and significantly lower for older respondents (above 45 years) (OR of interaction: 0.68, 95% CI: 0.61–0.76, p-value <0.001).
evidence: The claim presents specific statistical results from the heterogeneity analysis for education.

claim: The odds of choosing the candidate from the Global South were significantly lower for older respondents above 45 years (OR of interaction: 0.68, 95% CI: 0.61–0.76, p<0.001).
source: The odds of choosing the candidate from the Global South rather than the candidate from the respondents' own country (all else equal) were significantly higher for female (OR of interaction: 1.22, 95% CI: 1.10–1.36, p-value <0.001) and more educated (OR of interaction: 1.63, 95% CI: 1.46–1.82, p-value <0.001) respondents, and significantly lower for older respondents (above 45 years) (OR of interaction: 0.68, 95% CI: 0.61–0.76, p-value <0.001).
evidence: The claim presents specific statistical results from the heterogeneity analysis for age.

claim: Respondents who were themselves at high risk of a severe COVID-19 disease progression were significantly less supportive of distributing the COVID-19 vaccine to a candidate from the Global South (OR of interaction: 0.70, 95% CI: 0.63–0.78, p<0.001).
source: Further, respondents who were themselves at high risk of a severe COVID-19 disease progression were significantly less supportive of distributing the COVID-19 vaccine to a candidate from the Global South (OR of interaction: 0.70, 95% CI: 0.63–0.78, p-value <0.001).
evidence: The claim presents specific statistical results from the heterogeneity analysis for COVID-19 risk status.

claim: In the subgroup of employed respondents, the odds of distributing the vaccine to a candidate in the Global South were slightly lower than in the subgroup of respondents that are not employed (OR of interaction: 0.89, 95% CI: 0.80–1.00, p=0.045).
source: In the subgroup of employed respondents, the odds of distributing the vaccine to a candidate in the Global South were slightly lower than in the subgroup of respondents that are not employed (OR of interaction: 0.89, 95% CI: 0.80–1.00, p-value = 0.045).
evidence: The claim presents specific statistical results from the heterogeneity analysis for employment status.

claim: The degree of COVID-19 threat perception did not significantly affect respondents' distribution preferences (OR of interaction: 1.10, 95% CI: 0.99–1.22, p=0.071).
source: The degree of COVID-19 threat perception did not seem to significantly affect respondents' distribution preferences (OR of interaction with a dummy variable indicating a high threat perception: 1.10, 95% CI: 0.99–1.22, p-value = 0.071).
evidence: The claim presents specific statistical results from the heterogeneity analysis for threat perception.

claim: Respondents living in a region with a higher COVID-19 case incidence were on average slightly less supportive of distributing the vaccine to a candidate from the Global South (OR of interaction: 0.998, 95% CI: 0.997–0.998, p<0.001).
source: When including the subnational COVID-19 incidence as a continuous heterogeneity variable, we found that respondents living in a region with a higher case incidence were on average slightly less supportive of distributing the vaccine to a candidate from the Global South (OR of interaction: 0.998, 95% CI: 0.997–0.998, p-value <0.001; see Supplementary file 1k).
evidence: The claim presents specific statistical results from the subnational heterogeneity analysis.

claim: Vaccine allocation preferences are largely driven by the assessed vulnerability of possible recipients, irrespective of whether the recipient lives in the respondents' own country or in the Global South.
source: Our results suggest that vaccine allocation preferences are largely driven by the assessed vulnerability of possible recipients, irrespective of whether the recipient lives in the respondents' own country or in the Global South.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the study's results.

claim: Respondents prioritise the candidate with the higher mortality risk but a foreign nationality over the candidate with a lower mortality risk but with the same nationality.
source: For example, they prioritise the candidate with the higher mortality risk but a foreign nationality over the candidate with a lower mortality risk but with the same nationality.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the study's results.

claim: Respondents prioritise vaccine receipt according to the extent at which a candidate's employment status and income generation is affected by the pandemic situation.
source: Thus, respondents seem to prioritise vaccine receipt according to the extent at which a candidate's employment status – and income generation – is affected by the pandemic situation.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the study's results.

claim: Studies have repeatedly found in-group bias (or national bias) in distributional preferences.
source: First, studies have repeatedly found in-group bias (or here: national bias) in distributional preferences (Bernhard et al., 2006; Reese et al., 2012; Yudkin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim cites literature on in-group bias.

claim: Several cross-country analyses have found German citizens to be among the least nationalistic in Europe.
source: We lack the data to test this possible explanation directly, but it seems unlikely: several cross-country analyses investigating nationalism, patriotism, and xenophobia have found German citizens to be among the least nationalistic in Europe (Coenders et al., 2021; Lubbers and Coenders, 2017).
evidence: The claim cites cross-country analyses on nationalism.

claim: German citizens do not generally appear to be outliers among their European peers in terms of altruism or similar pro-sociality variables.
source: German citizens also do not generally appear to be outliers among their European peers in terms of altruism or similar pro-sociality variables (Fehr et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim cites research on altruism and pro-sociality.

claim: When the survey was fielded in Italy, France, Spain, Poland, and Sweden, the vaccination rate in those countries exceeded 50% for first doses and 30% for second doses.
source: When the survey was fielded in Italy, France, Spain, Poland, and Sweden, the vaccination rate in those countries exceeded 50% (30%) for first (second) doses, whereas in Germany it was only at 25% (8%) (see Supplementary file 1l).
evidence: The claim provides vaccination rate data at the time of survey fielding.

claim: When the survey was fielded in Germany, the vaccination rate was only at 25% for first doses and 8% for second doses.
source: When the survey was fielded in Italy, France, Spain, Poland, and Sweden, the vaccination rate in those countries exceeded 50% (30%) for first (second) doses, whereas in Germany it was only at 25% (8%) (see Supplementary file 1l).
evidence: The claim provides vaccination rate data at the time of survey fielding in Germany.

claim: The differential findings for Germany are most likely driven by a combination of higher infection rates, lower vaccination rates at the time of data collection, and a higher proportion of older, high-risk and lower educated respondents in the German sample.
source: In view of the above, the differential findings for Germany are most likely driven by a combination of (i) higher infection and (ii) lower vaccination rates at the time of the German data collection and (iii) a higher proportion of older, high-risk and lower educated respondents in the German sample.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation and synthesis of multiple findings to explain the German results.

claim: The samples are not nationally representative of the population profile of each country due to the two eligibility criteria of not yet having been vaccinated and being willing to get vaccinated.
source: Finally, as a consequence of the two eligibility criteria of (1) not yet having been vaccinated against COVID-19 and (2) being willing to get vaccinated, our samples are not nationally representative of the population profile of each country (compare Table 1 with the census data in Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: The claim acknowledges a limitation of the study regarding sample representativeness.

claim: The suggested estimates of citizens' support for global solidarity in distributing the COVID-19 vaccines are most likely lower bound estimates.
source: In view of this, our suggested estimates of citizens' support for global solidarity in distributing the COVID-19 vaccines are most likely lower bound estimates – assuming that already vaccinated citizens and those less interested in getting vaccinated would be even more willing to donate vaccine doses to the Global South.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the likely direction of bias in the estimates.

claim: The World Health Organisation's call for a moratorium on COVID-19 booster vaccinations in high-income countries in favour of prioritising first dose vaccinations in low-income countries went unheeded.
source: Still, the World Health Organisation's call for a moratorium on COVID-19 booster vaccinations in high-income countries in favour of prioritising first dose vaccinations in low-income countries went unheeded, at least in part out of a sense that donating vaccines to countries in the Global South lacks popular support and might even subject the government to electoral punishment (Krause et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim states a fact about WHO's call and its reception, with a citation.

claim: The emergence of the Omicron variant and its various subvariants throughout 2022 emphasises the transboundary nature of the COVID-19 pandemic.
source: The emergence of the Omicron and its various subvariants throughout 2022, as well as ongoing concerns about potential future variants, emphasise once again the transboundary nature of the COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about the Omicron variant and its implications.

claim: Governments of European countries can rely on solid public approval for a more equitable vaccine distribution, especially among female, younger and more educated citizens.
source: Findings from our study suggest that governments of European countries can rely on solid public approval for a more equitable vaccine distribution – especially among female, younger and more educated citizens.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Public support for vaccine donations to the Global South may be even more pronounced at the time of writing, since COVID-19 risk groups have now already received their first or even second booster vaccination.
source: Public support for vaccine donations to the Global South may be even more pronounced at the time of writing, since COVID-19 risk groups have now already received their first (or even second) booster vaccination.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about current public support based on changed circumstances.

claim: Employment security is much lower in low- and middle-income countries, especially in view of the high share of workers in the informal sector.
source: Moreover, our finding regarding prioritising candidates according to employment status, and particularly potential income losses, may also indirectly point to a pronounced public support for vaccine donations to the Global South: Employment security is much lower in low- and middle-income countries, especially in view of the high share of workers in the informal sector, where substantial income losses are more likely to occur during a lockdown or pandemic-induced economic downturns.
evidence: The claim is based on general knowledge about employment in LMICs.

claim: More effective international policy initiatives to ensure efficient, adequate, and timely COVID-19 vaccine transfers to low-income countries are urgently needed.
source: More effective international policy initiatives to ensure efficient, adequate, and timely COVID-19 vaccine transfers to low-income countries are therefore urgently needed.
evidence: The claim is a policy recommendation based on the study's findings.
